sections.title: Executive summary

summary.text: The executive summary of the consolidated HIV strategic information guidelines notes that despite abundant data, new infections remain above targets and retention and late diagnosis are problems. It explains that the guidelines focus on individual-level routine data to strengthen person-centred services and linkage to prevention and treatment. It also notes the inclusion of data on STIs, TB, viral hepatitis and cervical cancer in HIV data systems.

sections.title: Evolving data needs for a new phase of the HIV response

summary.text: Describes progress in the HIV response, with about 28 million of 38 million people living with HIV on treatment in 2021, and new challenges such as loss to follow-up and slow declines in new infections. It argues that routine data systems must evolve to identify gaps faster, alongside surveys, studies and models, while keeping the people whose data are gathered safe and their data secure.

sections.extract: Enormous gains have been made in the HIV response over the four decades since the first identification of the virus. Treatment has expanded to an estimated 28 million people of the 38 million people living with HIV in 2021, and eight countries have achieved the UNAIDS 90–90–90 targets (1). sections.title: Advancing from aggregate to individual-level data use

summary.text: Contrasts aggregate facility data with individual-level data, explaining that person-level records linked by unique identifiers improve continuity of care, reduce duplicate counts and allow more accurate automated reporting. It describes how paper-based and electronic reporting may run in parallel while systems mature and be combined at subnational or national level. It stresses checking completeness and quality and the principle of collecting data once and using it many times.

sections.extract: The major source of strategic information used to monitor the HIV response in the health sector is aggregate routine facility data. sections.title: Epidemiology of HIV and prevention need

summary.text: Describes slow declines in HIV incidence, with 1.5 million new infections in 2020, and the rising share among key populations and their partners. It notes that criminalization, stigma and discrimination create barriers that must be addressed for equitable access to prevention.

sections.title: Strategic information for HIV prevention

summary.text: Explains why HIV prevention outcomes are hard to measure, since people start and stop prevention as needs change, and why multiple data sources are needed. The guidelines focus on routine programmatic data, which can also identify people at elevated risk and track whether interventions are received and used.

sections.extract: Measuring HIV prevention programmes against health outcomes (such as individuals remaining HIV-negative or new HIV infections) can be challenging. sections.title: HIV prevention interventions

summary.text: Advocates a person-centred, context-specific approach to HIV prevention delivered through varied settings, including community-led services, in line with the Global AIDS Strategy. It lists evidence-based biomedical and health-sector prevention interventions, from ART and PrEP to needle–syringe programmes and male circumcision, and notes that counselling alone has not shown an effect on incidence. It points to tools for setting prevention targets for key populations.

sections.extract: A person-centred approach should address the range of HIV prevention and other health needs that individuals might have and make appropriate interventions available in a manner acceptable to them. The design of HIV prevention programmes should be informed by the local context and the nature of the local HIV epidemic and tailored to meet the HIV prevention needs of the individuals and communities they serve. summary.text: Discusses how intersecting factors such as age, gender and criminalization shape HIV risk and access to prevention, and how individual risk changes over time. sections.title: Understanding person-centred HIV prevention need

summary.text: Describes how client–provider conversations, held with privacy and often with peer support, help identify an individual's HIV prevention needs, and stresses offering prevention to anyone who asks without requiring explanation. It covers the use of prevention prioritization or risk assessment tools when people underestimate their risk, especially adolescents. It advises reassessing need regularly and gives example screening questions to adapt locally.

sections.extract: Conversations between service providers and clients during a consultation are key to understanding an individual’s HIV prevention needs. Such conversations may take place before or after HIV testing, during a sexual health consultation, or when providing HIV prevention services. It notes that trans and gender diverse people can be identified from data on sex assigned at birth and current gender identity.

sections.title: A minimum dataset for HIV prevention

summary.text: Recommends collecting a minimum set of individual-level data for each HIV prevention intervention, using event dates to show what happened and when, on paper or electronic tools. A table sets out the minimum dataset for interventions such as HIV testing, condoms, PrEP, needle–syringe programmes, opioid agonist maintenance treatment and voluntary medical male circumcision.

sections.extract: In the course of delivering each HIV prevention intervention, collection of a minimum set of individual-level data is suggested (Table 2.2). In this minimum dataset, the date that an event occurs (for example, date of HIV test, date PrEP prescribed, etc.) serves to indicate that the event occurred as well as when it occurred. These data can be collected at the point where an HIV prevention intervention is provided.

summary.text: Explains why HIV prevention cascades are harder to build than treatment cascades, since interventions are delivered in varied ways, risk changes over time, outcomes are non-linear and commodities come from many sources. It points to existing frameworks, including a PAHO approach for key populations, and advises reading prevention cascades alongside testing and treatment cascades.

sections.title: Purpose of person-centred monitoring of HIV testing, treatment and care

summary.text: Defines HIV patient monitoring as routinely gathering, analysing and using data about people with HIV across services and over time, mainly to guide clinical care and ensure continuity of testing and treatment. It lists further uses of the data, such as tracking epidemic trends, measuring programme performance and informing drug stock management to reduce wastage and stock-outs.

sections.extract: treatment and care HIV patient monitoring encompasses the routine collection, compilation, analysis and use of data on people living with HIV over time and across service delivery points. summary.text: Describes how investments in digital health information systems, electronic medical records and unique identifiers have strengthened person-centred monitoring and led to a prioritized minimum dataset. It explains that the chapter updates WHO's 2017 patient monitoring guidance to cover the full care cascade and support differentiated service delivery. It also notes the expansion from 40 to 80 priority indicators, of which 36 come from patient monitoring and 25 are core, plus optional additional indicators for countries with stronger systems.

sections.extract: The investments that countries have made in digital HIS, including electronic medical records (EMRs) and the adoption of UIDs, has strengthened person-centred patient monitoring and service delivery. sections.title: Application of this guidance

summary.text: Explains that the updated guidance supports monitoring people as they move between facilities, recommending facility-held patient cards, ART registers or electronic records with data flowing in from community services, as well as new tools for differentiated service delivery. It describes the intended audiences and notes that pharmacy services and non-HIV TB and maternal and child health data elements are outside its scope.

sections.extract: The updated guidance in this chapter seeks particularly to support monitoring of people living with HIV as they move between health facilities over time. sections.title: HIV testing services, early diagnosis and linkage to treatment

summary.text: A box summarizing new WHO HIV testing recommendations relevant to patient monitoring, including testing all pregnant women for HIV, syphilis and hepatitis B, dual HIV/syphilis rapid tests in antenatal care and differing approaches for high- and low-burden settings. It also covers self-testing, index and network-based testing and the need to update tools and records to track linkage between facilities and community services.

sections.title: Purposes of monitoring testing

summary.text: Explains that understanding people's HIV testing history and results guides their care and that monitoring should cover all prevention, testing and treatment service points. It outlines the purposes of testing data, such as optimizing case finding and linkage to ART and prevention, and presents a table of six priority HIV testing indicators. It ends with guidance on which partners and family members of index clients should be offered testing.

sections.extract: Understanding HIV testing history, patterns of testing, retesting and test results is necessary to guide the provision of support and clinical care to clients. Patient monitoring systems, whether paper-based or electronic, can facilitate effective clinical management and also generate data for programme monitoring. Increasing number of people living with HIV who know their status

summary.text: Notes that as more people living with HIV know their status, test positivity falls and reaching undiagnosed people becomes harder, making analysis of routine testing data essential. It explains how unique identifiers enable tracking along the care continuum and introduces indicators on test volume and positivity and on individuals testing positive.

sections.title: Early HIV diagnosis

summary.text: Highlights early diagnosis as key to treatment success and reduced transmission, recommending monitoring of CD4 count and disease stage at diagnosis to detect late presenters. It stresses self-testing and community and network-based testing with timely linkage, supported by interoperable data systems and community-led monitoring.

sections.extract: Early diagnosis is key to treatment success, improved patient outcomes and reduced onward HIV transmission. New diagnoses likely reflect a mix of those newly identified with HIV infection, those previously diagnosed but not linked to care and those previously diagnosed but disengaged from HIV treatment and care services. Monitoring CD4 count and disease stage at diagnosis is important to identify late diagnoses, as

sections.title: Linkage to treatment and care

summary.text: Explains that prompt linkage to treatment improves viral suppression and reduces resistance, illness, death and transmission, and that it includes re-engaging people who have dropped out of care. It describes the core linkage indicator measuring the share of newly diagnosed people who start ART, disaggregated by time since diagnosis. It also covers partner and contact testing services with consent and confidentiality, their cascade data, and a survey-based indicator on key populations who know their status.

sections.extract: Linkage to treatment and care is the first step toward onward services, including timely initiation of ART as well as access to interventions to prevent the further transmission of HIV, to prevent other infections and to manage co-morbidities. Linkage to treatment and care is essential to achieve programmatic impact and effective patient management and care. Delays in ART linkage are associated with lower levels of

sections.title: Standardized data collection tools for HTS

summary.text: Notes that the annexes include examples of standardized HIV testing data collection tools from Malawi, such as testing, screening, confirmatory and self-test distribution registers.

sections.extract: Annexes provide examples of countries’ standardized data collection tools for HTS. These include an HTS register (Web Annex C), digital scan forms that include an HTS initial screening register (Web Annex F), an HTS confirmatory register (Web Annex E) and an HIVST distribution register (Web Annex D) from Malawi.

sections.title: Minimum dataset

summary.text: Lists the minimum HIV testing data to record consistently across facility and community sites: test date, result, date of diagnosis, date the result was received and linkage to care where feasible.

sections.extract: Data collection practices and completeness of records may vary across settings and testing approaches. Where possible, HIV testing information should be collected in a standardized manner across all service sites, including at the facility and community levels. At a minimum the following information should be recorded: • HIV test date • HIV test result • date of diagnosis • date that client received the result •

sections.title: ART initiation, retention and viral suppression

summary.text: A box summarizing new WHO HIV treatment recommendations relevant to patient monitoring, such as rapid and same-day ART initiation, updated first-, second- and third-line regimens and a revised viral load monitoring algorithm. It notes that patient tools, electronic records and the minimum dataset must be updated accordingly, including for revised antiretroviral toxicity indicators covering weight gain, cardiometabolic effects and adverse pregnancy outcomes.

sections.extract: Box 3.3 What’s new in HIV treatment relevant to HIV patient monitoring • Rapid initiation and same-day start of ART: Since 2017 WHO has recommended that ART should be offered to all people living with HIV following a confirmed HIV diagnosis and clinical assessment within seven days of diagnosis and preferably on the same day as confirmed HIV diagnosis, for people who are ready to start ART (11). sections.title: What to monitor and relevant treatment indicators

summary.text: Explains that under WHO's treat-all policy, people on ART must be monitored over time as they move between facilities, with priority treatment indicators tracking the cascade from initiation or re-entry to retention, viral suppression, discontinuation, toxicity, loss to follow-up and death. It presents a table of these indicators, starting with ART coverage towards the second 95 target and total attrition. It describes updates to the attrition indicator and invites country feedback on its feasibility.

sections.extract: In the context of current WHO “treat all” recommendations, it remains critical to monitor people living with HIV who receive ART over time as they move between health facilities and access care at different service delivery points. Priority indicators for HIV treatment focus on monitoring the treatment cascade from ART initiation and/or re-entry into treatment through to treatment outcomes that include retention, VL

sections.title: Monitoring ART initiation, late initiation and clinical management

summary.text: Stresses person-centred ART initiation and introduces the indicators on new ART patients and late initiation, with a table of WHO recommendations on when to start ART, including rapid and same-day initiation and exceptions. It covers monitoring of clinical management and lists paediatric monitoring priorities such as early infant diagnosis coverage and age at diagnosis and treatment start. It also notes the need for fine age disaggregation of testing and treatment indicators.

sections.extract: management ART initiation should follow the overarching principles of providing person-centred care. Person-centred care should be focused and organized around the health needs, preferences and expectations of people and communities. Likewise, patient monitoring should also be person-centred and enable longitudinal monitoring of people living with HIV as they access HIV treatment and care services and, where

sections.title: Monitoring treatment outcomes

summary.text: Describes updates to viral load monitoring, with the first test reviewed by six months after starting ART and a repeat test three months after an unsuppressed result following enhanced adherence counselling. It distinguishes treatment failure above 1,000 copies/mL from lower detectable levels and presents WHO's 2021 viral load testing algorithm with actions for each result.

sections.extract: Viral suppression A number of updates have been made to the treatment monitoring algorithm. First, the initial VL test should be collected and tested, and the result should be reviewed, by the time of the six-month visit after ART initiation. sections.title: ART retention/attrition

summary.text: Explains that retention on ART is key to viral suppression and lower mortality, citing sub-Saharan African data showing nearly one fifth stopped ART and 15–20% died within five years. It describes monitoring attrition and the role of unique identifiers in tracking people between facilities and avoiding miscounting of silent transfers.

sections.extract: The main function of an ART programme, after initiation, is to support retention in treatment and adherence in order to achieve viral suppression and so reduce mortality. Long-term retention in care is a key challenge, with impacts on patient health, the emergence of HIV drug resistance and onward transmission of HIV. sections.title: Loss to follow-up

summary.text: Calls for analysis of attrition data to find facilities needing support and the causes of poor retention, from waiting times to drug toxicity. It explains that people counted as lost to follow-up are often silent transfers, deaths or discontinuations, and describes data-driven tracing and re-engagement, criteria for tracing and an updated patient card recording prior ARV exposure and restarts. It also mentions monitoring ART initiation alongside treatment interruption as people return to care.

In addition, these data should be analysed to identify facilities that need support and the reasons for retention problems, including health system issues (long waiting times, quality of service), sociodemographic issues and client- and treatment-related factors (for example, ARV toxicity). sections.title: Advanced HIV disease

summary.text: Defines advanced HIV disease as a CD4 count below 200 cells/mm³ or WHO clinical stage 3 or 4 in adults and adolescents, and all children under five living with HIV, noting these people need closer follow-up. It describes the package of screening, prophylaxis and rapid ART recommended for advanced disease and the data elements to monitor it. It also stresses resource planning and monitoring for immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome and adverse drug reactions.

sections.extract: Advanced HIV disease in adults and adolescents is defined by a CD4 cell count of less than 200 cells/mm3 and/or WHO clinical stage 3 or 4 disease (2). All children younger than five years of age living with HIV are considered to have advanced HIV disease. People with advanced HIV disease are at greater risk of mortality and require closer follow-up during the initial period of ART to monitor the response to

sections.title: ARV toxicity monitoring

summary.text: Explains why monitoring ARV drug safety is increasingly important as treatment scales up and newer drugs are introduced, including for pregnant and breastfeeding women. It describes WHO's recommended combination of approaches, such as pregnancy safety surveillance and active and routine toxicity monitoring. A table lists data elements for monitoring weight gain and cardiometabolic toxicity, including risk factors and drug exposure.

sections.extract: As ART scale-up continues, with earlier and more prolonged exposure to treatment, and with the transition to new ARVs among all age groups including pregnant and breastfeeding women, monitoring the safety of ARV drugs has become a critical component of HIV treatment and prevention programmes. Newer ARVs have more favourable toxicity profiles and provide an opportunity to standardize and optimize HIV treatment.

sections.title: Early warning indicators of HIV drug resistance

summary.text: Describes early warning indicators of HIV drug resistance, a set of quality-of-care measures used to identify clinics where service gaps could foster resistance. It reviews viral, drug, patient and programme factors linked to resistance and presents a table of the current indicators and targets. It also describes a WHO tool for collecting and reporting the indicators and urges countries to use routine patient monitoring rather than parallel systems.

sections.extract: The early warning indicators (EWIs) are a set of standard quality-of-care indicators used to assess whether ART programmes deliver services of sufficient quality to minimize the emergence of HIV drug resistance. The EWIs use standardized definitions that have evolved over time as programmes mature and public health actions are refined (Table 3.5). sections.title: Monitoring considerations for paediatric populations

summary.text: Sets out general child health monitoring for children living with HIV, such as growth, development, immunization and infant feeding, noting WHO guidance that mothers on ART with suppressed viral loads can breastfeed up to two years. It lists additional paediatric indicators, including viral suppression by age, psychosocial support and optimized second-line regimens, and stresses continuity of records as children move into adolescent and adult care.

sections.extract: Monitoring for children includes general and HIV-specific monitoring. Age disaggregation (five-year intervals) is important, as interventions may depend on age. sections.title: Monitoring vertical transmission

summary.text: Summarizes what is new in monitoring vertical transmission of HIV, including stronger tracking of the PMTCT cascade across services and over the full exposure period and an emphasis on elimination. It describes the priority indicator on viral suppression at labour and delivery and recent WHO recommendations relevant to pregnant and breastfeeding women. It explains that these changes require updates to patient monitoring tools and indicators.

summary.text: Outlines the conceptual framework for monitoring PMTCT across multiple services and over a long period, from primary prevention and reproductive health services to treating mothers and following exposed infants to final diagnosis.

summary.text: Explains that data tools must follow mother–baby pairs between service points and facilities, relying on unique identifiers, integration of HIV information into maternal and child health cards or electronic systems. It recommends integrating PMTCT and paediatric HIV services and their monitoring with maternal, newborn and child health care.

summary.text: Describes the updated vertical transmission indicators, which since 2020 emphasize results like maternal viral suppression and early diagnosis of infants, with seven designated national priority indicators tied to key points in the risk period. summary.text: Stresses following mother–infant pairs from antenatal and delivery care to child health and ART services, using a mother–infant pair register and recording the mother's identifier on the infant's record. It lists the care HIV-exposed infants should receive and be monitored for, such as prophylaxis, timely nucleic acid testing, feeding practices and final outcome testing. It sets out the minimum dataset for exposed infants, highlighting updates since 2017.

sections.extract: Strengthening follow-up of mother–infant pairs, from ANC, labour and delivery (maternity) and postpartum maternal visits to child health clinics and ART services, remains critical for elimination of vertical transmission and improved maternal and child health outcomes. sections.title: Monitoring TB/HIV

summary.text: Summarizes 2020 updates to TB–HIV patient monitoring, including revised indicators on TB preventive treatment and rapid molecular TB testing and new shorter preventive regimens. It recalls WHO's collaborative TB/HIV activities and lists recent recommendations relevant to recording and reporting, such as new screening tools and starting ART within two weeks of TB treatment.

summary.text: Calls for strong coordination, referral and communication between TB and HIV services, supported by electronic systems and co-located clinics, to ensure joint care and reconciled records. It tabulates TB–HIV data elements for HIV patient cards and registers. It also lists additional HIV data elements recommended for TB treatment cards, such as unique identifier, CD4 count, viral load and ARV regimen.

sections.title: Introduction

summary.text: Introduces WHO's 2021 service delivery recommendations for HIV treatment and care, aimed at improving access, simplifying care and supporting return to care. It notes that the section presents eight key recommendations supporting differentiated service delivery and its monitoring.

sections.extract: In 2021 WHO released updated recommendations on treatment and care service delivery for people living with HIV (3) with a series of recommendations and good practice statements intended to promote continued improvements in access to ART, to simplify care delivery for providers and end users and to support return to care for those who have disengaged (Box 3.15). sections.title: Overview of DSD

summary.text: Defines differentiated service delivery as a person-centred approach that adapts HIV services to people's needs while using resources efficiently, built on four elements: what, where, who and when. It describes four categories of differentiated ART models, from health worker-managed groups to individual facility and community models. It summarizes WHO recommendations on less frequent visits and refills, community delivery and task sharing with nurses, community health workers and lay providers.

sections.extract: DSD is a person-centred approach that simplifies and adapts HIV services across the care and treatment cascade to reflect the needs and preferences of people living with HIV or vulnerable to infection. sections.title: Monitoring DSD

summary.text: Explains that patient monitoring systems and tools must be adapted to capture data from differentiated service delivery models, with updated patient cards, registers and reports. It stresses that the linked facility keeps clinical responsibility and that community site data should be entered promptly into facility systems to avoid parallel reporting and support tracking of missed pick-ups.

summary.text: Notes that the key indicators for differentiated service delivery cover coverage, uptake and clinical outcomes, but that programme management also needs measures of client and worker experience, costs, efficiency and workload. It points to forthcoming WHO guidance and an existing ICAP framework for monitoring and evaluation.

summary.text: Explains why collecting identifiable data on stigmatized or criminalized behaviours from people on ART can harm clients and providers, through law enforcement use, underreporting and discrimination. It notes that behaviours change over time, so labelling someone as a key population member may not stay meaningful.

sections.extract: Data relating to an individual’s behaviours can be important for patient management and programme monitoring. Partner-related prevention interventions can be noted on the back of the patient card.

sections.extract: While HIV prevention services can be provided without the need to collect personally identifying information and using anonymous UID codes to allow longitudinal monitoring, in most settings it is required that individuals receiving HIV treatment are identified. It describes how key population programmes can confirm linkage to treatment while protecting identities, with an example from the EpiC programme in Malawi using triplicate referral tickets.

sections.title: Minimum dataset and key definitions for HIV patient monitoring

summary.text: Introduces the minimum dataset for HIV patient monitoring, a standardized set of demographic, clinical and laboratory data elements with defined coding, and highlights new elements in the 2022 version. It notes WHO's recommendation of rapid ART initiation within seven days of diagnosis.

summary.text: States WHO's recommendation that everyone starting ART be entered in a longitudinal ART register organized by start cohort and used to compile cohort and cross-sectional reports. It explains benefits for integrated settings and lists updates to the register, such as DSD enrolment, weight gain as a toxicity and fluconazole prophylaxis.

sections.title: Background and rationale

summary.text: Sets out the rationale for measuring quality of care, citing estimates that poor-quality care causes millions of deaths and huge economic losses in low- and middle-income countries. It argues that people receiving HIV services need high-quality care, that quality must be measured across health system levels, and that WHO quality definitions should be used locally.

sections.extract: Each year poor-quality care contributes to 5.7–8.4 million deaths from all causes in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), comprising 15% of total deaths in these countries (5). More lives are lost due to poor-quality care than to lack of access to health care (6). In addition to the tremendous loss of life, annual economic losses associated with poor quality care are enormous, exceeding US$ 6 trillion (6).

sections.title: Measuring QOC

summary.text: Describes how quality of HIV care should be measured mainly through existing information systems and routine data, with a framework that defines data sources, capacity, triangulation and use for improvement. It stresses capturing integrated, longitudinal care across service points, considering the diversity of clients and keeping data anonymised. The section also notes related services, such as palliative and psychosocial care, that should be considered when measuring quality.

sections.extract: Ideally, QOC is measured through existing strategic information systems. Thus, QOC data depend on the strength of national health management information systems.
